title: What does an unbalanced force do?

title: What does an unbalanced force do?
summary: An unbalanced force changes an object's motion, in the direction of the net force. Speeding up, slowing down, stopping, reversing and turning are all changes in motion, and every one needs an unbalanced force.
language: science
voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 }
app:
  command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8202
  url: http://127.0.0.1:8202/index.html
  readySelector: "#gpanel"
  layout: full
explainPicture: { ref: boards.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Net force 2 N to the left: the motion changes towards the left, whichever way the puck was moving." }
explainClip:
  query: { code: "@boards.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain }
  caption: "What an unbalanced force does"
  say: "An unbalanced force changes the motion, in the direction of the net force."
  clip:
    - caption: { text: "A puck slides right. A push to the left keeps acting on it.", say: "A puck slides right on ice, while a push to the left keeps acting." }
    - click: "Play"
    - wait: 1600
    - caption: { text: "First it slows down…", say: "First it slows down." }
    - wait: 900
    - caption: { text: "…stops, then speeds up to the left.", say: "It stops, and then speeds up to the left." }
    - expect: { selector: "body", contains: "speed -" }
    - caption: { text: "One unbalanced force: slowing, stopping and reversing are all one change.", say: "Slowing, stopping and reversing are all changes caused by one unbalanced force." }
    - wait: 800
hook: "A curling stone glides 40 metres across the ice. Sweep in front of it and it slides further; let it hit another stone and it stops dead. Every time its motion changes, something has pushed or pulled it."

You've seen that balanced forces leave an object's motion just as it was, so what happens when one push or pull is bigger than the other?

## Engage: the sliding puck

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Students readily link a net force to speeding up, but expect a backward force only to stop things; the board shows the same force slowing, stopping and reversing the puck."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "A puck slides to the right across smooth ice. A steady push to the left starts acting on it and keeps acting. What do you predict happens?"
  options: ["It stops straight away", "It slows down and stops, then stays still", "It slows down, stops, then moves off to the left, faster and faster", "It keeps sliding right at the same speed: it is already moving"]
  actual: "It slows down, stops, then moves off to the left, faster and faster. The net force points left the whole time, so the motion keeps changing towards the left: first slower, then reversed."
```

## Explore: push against the motion

```step
stage: run
insight: "One steady force producing three different-looking changes (slowing, stopping, reversing) is the evidence that all of them are one effect: a change in motion towards the net force."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#puck", height: 640 }
check: { type: board, text: "With a push to the left, make the puck turn round and move to the left.", when: "t >= 1 and v < 0" }
```

The puck starts moving right at 4 m/s, and the ice has no friction. Press **Play** and watch the dots and the speed–time graph: a speed below zero means moving to the left. Try a bigger and a smaller push (**Reset** to start again).

## Explain: any change in motion

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Widening 'change in motion' from speeding up to slowing, stopping, reversing and turning is the node's checkpoint: any change in motion needs an unbalanced force."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "On the board, why did the puck turn round?"
      options: ["The push kept acting: the net force pointed left, so the puck slowed, stopped and then sped up to the left", "The puck ran out of the force that was carrying it right", "The push only started working once the puck had stopped"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Nothing was carrying it to the right, because on frictionless ice it would slide on forever, so what did the push do?", "Look at the graph, because the speed started falling the moment the push acted."]
      explain: "An unbalanced force changes the motion in the direction of the net force for as long as it acts, so slowing down, stopping and reversing were all the same change, towards the left."
    hint: ["Imagine the same puck on the ice with nothing pushing it at all. What would it do?", "Watch the speed-time graph from the moment the push starts, and ask whether anything waits until the puck has stopped."]
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Is the motion changing? (If it is, there must be an unbalanced force.)"
      options: ["Changing: unbalanced force", "Not changing: balanced forces"]
      items:
        - ["A cyclist braking at the lights", "Changing: unbalanced force"]
        - ["A car going round a roundabout at a steady 30 km/h", "Changing: unbalanced force", "Its speed is steady but its direction keeps changing, and that counts as a change in motion."]
        - ["A lift rising at a steady speed", "Not changing: balanced forces"]
        - ["A ball thrown upwards, slowing as it rises", "Changing: unbalanced force", "Weight pulls it down the whole time, so it slows, stops at the top and then falls."]
        - ["A book resting on a desk", "Not changing: balanced forces"]
        - ["A netball changing direction when it bounces off the backboard", "Changing: unbalanced force"]
        - ["A train sitting at a platform", "Not changing: balanced forces"]
    hint: ["For each one, picture its path and its speed, and ask whether either of them is changing.", "Watch out for the ones where only one of those two is changing."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A car drives round a bend at a steady 40 km/h. Are the forces on it balanced?"
      options: ["No: its direction is changing, so there is a net force towards the inside of the bend", "Yes: its speed isn't changing", "There are no forces on it"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "A steady speed in a straight line means balanced forces, but is the car going in a straight line?", "The road grips the tyres, or the car would just slide straight on."]
      explain: "A change of direction is a change in motion, so it needs an unbalanced force, and here that's the tyres' grip on the road pulling the car towards the inside of the bend."
    hint: ["Is the car travelling in a straight line as it goes round the bend?", "Picture the car on really slippery ice: if the tyres couldn't grip, where would it go?"]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A cyclist rides to the right and is slowing down. Which force diagram fits?"
      options: ["Forward push 40 N to the right, air resistance and friction 70 N to the left", "Forward push 70 N to the right, air resistance and friction 40 N to the left", "Forward push 50 N to the right, air resistance and friction 50 N to the left", "No forward push, and no other forces"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "A net force to the right would speed her up, and that's not what's happening.", "Equal and opposite forces are balanced, and that would give a steady speed.", "With no forces at all she would keep going at the same speed, but there are forces here."]
      explain: "Slowing down while moving right means there's a net force to the left, because the backward arrow is longer: 70 N − 40 N = 30 N to the left."
    hint: ["Work out which way the net force has to point for her to be slowing down, and then look for the option that gives you that.", "For each option, take the smaller force from the bigger one and see which side is left over."]
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I explained, with a force diagram, why the puck slowed, stopped and turned round, and named a change in motion that is only a change of direction." }
```

In your book: draw force diagrams for two changes in motion, one where the speed changes and one where only the direction changes. Under each, name the unbalanced force.

## Mix it up

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Whether forces are unbalanced is read off the arrows, so the force diagram of a resting object comes back first."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Looking back at force arrows: a box rests on a table. Which arrows go in its force diagram?"
  options: ["Weight down and support up, the same length", "Only weight, pointing down", "Weight down, longer than the support up", "Weight and support, both pointing down"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "The table pushes back up, because support is a force too.", "If the weight arrow were longer, the box would sink into the table, but the two forces are equal.", "The table pushes up on the box, because support always points away from the surface."]
  explain: "Equal forces get arrows of equal length, and since weight points down and support points up, the two arrows balance."
```

## Elaborate: from standing still

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "Starting from rest with friction adds the third kind of change (starting) and makes students compare two arrows to find the net force before predicting."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#start", height: 640 }
tasks:
  - check: { type: board, text: "The box is at rest on a rough floor. Set the push so it starts moving to the right.", when: "t >= 1 and v > 0" }
    hint: ["Why doesn't the box move straight away with the push at 2 N?", "Slide the push up a bit at a time, watch the friction arrow and the line under the board, and press Play to check."]
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "The push is 7 N to the right and friction is 4 N to the left. What is the net force, in newtons?"
      answer: 3
      explain: "7 N − 4 N = 3 N to the right, so the forces are unbalanced and the box speeds up to the right, whereas with a push of 4 N or less, friction matches the push and the box stays still."
    hint: ["The two forces act in opposite directions along the same line. How would you combine them to see what's left over?", "Draw it as two arrows and ask how much longer the longer one is."]
```

## Elaborate: longer pushes

```step
stage: modify
tier: wider
insight: "A fair test and a First Peoples tool both turn on the same idea: the force, and how long it acts, decide how big the change in motion is."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "You want to test whether a bigger push changes a trolley's speed more quickly. Which plan is a fair test?"
      options: ["Use the same trolley on the same surface, and change only the size of the push", "Use a heavier trolley for the bigger push", "Push one trolley on carpet and the other on tiles"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "If you change the mass as well, you can't tell which change made the difference.", "Different surfaces give different friction, so that would mean two things changed."]
      explain: "You change one variable (the push), measure one (how quickly the speed changes) and keep the rest the same (trolley and surface)."
    hint: "Look at each plan and count how many things differ between the two trials, because that decides whether you can tell what caused the result."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A spearthrower lets the thrower keep pushing on the spear over a longer arc. Why does the spear leave faster?"
      options: ["The unbalanced force acts on the spear for longer, so its speed keeps increasing for longer", "The spearthrower makes the spear lighter", "The spearthrower stores the spear's speed and releases it"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "The spear's mass doesn't change, so that can't be the reason.", "Nothing is stored up, because the speed builds up while the push acts."]
      explain: "The longer an unbalanced force acts, the more the motion changes. Spearthrowers, used by First Peoples across much of mainland Australia, extend the throwing arm so the push lasts longer."
    hint: "Think about what happens to the spear's speed for as long as the thrower is still pushing on it."
```

## Evaluate: look back

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I compared my prediction about the sliding puck with what the board showed." }
```

Write one sentence: "At first I thought… Now I think… because…"

**Revision summary**

- An **unbalanced** force (a net force that isn't zero) **changes the motion**, in the direction of the net force.
- A change in motion can be **starting, speeding up, slowing down, stopping, reversing or changing direction**. Every one needs an unbalanced force.
- A force against the motion doesn't just stop an object: if it keeps acting, the object turns round and speeds up the other way.
- Steady speed round a bend is still a change in motion (direction), so the forces are unbalanced.

```teacher
summary: Students explain that unbalanced forces change motion (starting,
  speeding up, slowing down, stopping, reversing and changing direction) and
  represent each change with a force diagram (AC9S7U04, node 3).
time: 25
timing: Engage and Explore 8 min · Explain 10 min · Evaluate 3 min · Typical
  adds 4 min, Wider about 4 min
goals:
  - I can explain that an unbalanced force changes an object's motion, in the
    direction of the net force.
  - I can name speed and direction as the two things that can change.
  - I can draw force diagrams for two different changes in motion.
before: >
  A concept tutorial for introducing or revising the idea; it does not replace
  trolleys, force meters and ramps. Set the width with `?width=minimum`,
  `typical` (default) or `wider`.


  Not a hinge node, but its misconception is common: students apply "unbalanced
  force" to speeding up and miss slowing down, reversing and turning (and often
  think a backward force can only stop things). The Explore board shows one
  steady force slowing, stopping and reversing the puck. It builds on node 2
  (Balanced), so set that first.


  Board notes: the puck slides on frictionless ice and moves left and right
  only; turning and falling are covered by the sort and the round-the-bend
  question, not the board. Speeds below zero on the graph mean moving to the
  left. The Typical board has friction that matches the push up to 4 N while the
  box is still.
running:
  - "Engage: tally the predictions. 'Slows down and stops, then stays still' is
    the one to watch."
  - "Explore: ask what the graph does at the moment the speed crosses zero, and
    which way the net force points before and after."
  - "Explain: the sort is the checkpoint (the roundabout and the thrown ball are
    the hard ones); the diagram question asks for a force diagram."
  - "In your own words: two diagrams, one speed change and one direction change,
    are the node's success criteria."
struggle: Seeing slowing, stopping, reversing and turning as changes that need
  an unbalanced force. When a student says the puck ran out of force, ask what
  it would do on ice with no push at all.
stuck:
  - see: A student says the puck turned round because it ran out of force.
    ask: On ice with no push at all, what would the puck do?
    fix: Keep sliding at the same speed. Moving needs no force; changing the motion
      does. The push changed it.
  - see: A student says the car on the roundabout has balanced forces because its
      speed is steady.
    ask: Is it going in a straight line?
    fix: "No: its direction changes, so its motion changes, so the forces are
      unbalanced (the road pulls it towards the centre)."
  - see: A student thinks a force only acts while the object moves in its direction.
    ask: When did the speed start falling on the graph?
    fix: "The moment the push started: the force acts whichever way the puck is
      moving."
stretch: "A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top it is still for an
  instant. Is the force on it balanced at that moment? (No: weight still acts,
  which is why it falls.)"
support: "Give the sentence frame: 'The net force points … so the object …
  (speeds up, slows down, turns) …'."
leads: >
  Next: gravity, mass and weight (node 4). Node 5 (force, mass and the size of
  the change) is a class task: see the unit primer. In Year 10 this becomes
  Newton's first and second laws.


  In class: a trolley pulled by a force meter, then released against a rubber
  band; a ball rolled across the floor and tapped sideways with a ruler (a
  change of direction only).


  The spearthrower question (Wider) is general. For richer context, use local
  resources and community guidance about spearthrowers in your region.
exit:
  q: A netball flies towards the ring and bounces back off the backboard. Give the
    change in motion and the force that caused it.
  a: "It reversed direction (and slowed, then sped up the other way). The
    backboard pushed it back: an unbalanced force away from the board."
explain: >
  An **unbalanced** force changes an object's motion, in the direction of the
  net force: it can start, speed up, slow down, stop, reverse or turn an object.


  A force against the motion doesn't only stop things: if it keeps acting, the
  object turns round and speeds up the other way. A steady speed round a bend is
  a change in direction, so it needs an unbalanced force too.
```
